landmarks.name: Minaret of Jam
landmarks.writeup: A UNESCO World Heritage site, this 12th-century minaret is notable for its intricate brickwork and historical significance.

wiki.extract: The Minaret of Jam is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in western Afghanistan. It is located in a remote and nearly inaccessible region of Shahrak District, Ghor Province, between the Jam and Hari Rivers. The 62 m (203 ft) or 65 m (213 ft) high minaret was built c. 1190, entirely of baked bricks, and is famous for its intricate brick, stucco and glazed tile decoration, which consists of alternating bands of Kufic and Naskhi calligraphy, geometric patterns, and verses from the Qur'an. Since 2002, the minaret has remained on the list of World Heritage in Danger, under serious threat of erosion, and has not been actively preserved. In 2014, the BBC reported that the tower was in imminent danger of collapse.

landmarks.name: Bamiyan Buddhas (site)
landmarks.writeup: Once home to giant Buddha statues carved into cliffs, destroyed in 2001, the site remains culturally and historically important.

wiki.extract: The Buddhas of Bamiyan were two monumental Buddhist reliefs in the Bamiyan Valley of Afghanistan, carved possibly around the 6th-century. Located 130 kilometres (81 mi) to the northwest of Kabul, at an elevation of 2,500 metres (8,200 ft), carbon dating of the structural components of the Buddhas has determined the smaller 38 m (125 ft) "Eastern Buddha" was built around 570 CE, and the larger 55 m (180 ft) "Western Buddha" was built around 618 CE, which would date both to the time when the Hephthalites ruled the region.

landmarks.name: Band-e Amir National Park
landmarks.writeup: Afghanistan's first national park, known for its stunning series of deep blue lakes separated by natural dams.

wiki.extract: Band-e Amir National Park is located in the central Bamyan Province of Afghanistan. It was established on 22 May 2009 as Afghanistan's first national park to promote and protect the natural beauty of a series of intensely blue lakes created by natural dams high in the Hindu Kush. Band-e-Amir is a chain of six lakes in the southern mountainous desert area of the national park. The Balkh River originates here and flows to Balkh Province in the north.

cultural_events.name: Nowruz
cultural_events.writeup: Persian New Year celebrated on the spring equinox with traditional music, dance, and family gatherings.

wiki.extract: Nowruz is New Year's Day on the Iranian calendars, including the currently used Solar Hijri calendar. Historically, it has been observed by Iranian peoples, but is now celebrated by many Persianate cultures worldwide. It is a festival based on the Northern Hemisphere spring equinox, and thus usually coincides with a date between 19 March and 22 March on the Gregorian calendar.

cultural_events.name: Eid al-Fitr
cultural_events.writeup: A major Islamic festival marking the end of Ramadan, celebrated with prayers, feasts, and charity.

wiki.extract: Eid al-Fitr is the first of the two main festivals in Islam, the other being Eid al-Adha. The holiday falls on the first day of Shawwal, the tenth month of the Islamic calendar. One of the most important Islamic celebrations, Eid al-Fitr is celebrated by Muslims worldwide as it marks the end of the month-long, dawn-to-dusk fasting (sawm) during Ramadan. The holiday is known under various other names in different languages and countries around the world.

food_writeup: Afghan cuisine features rice dishes like Kabuli pulao, rich stews, flatbreads, and kebabs, reflecting Central Asian and Middle Eastern influences.
brief_history: Afghanistan has a history as a crossroads of civilizations, influenced by Persian, Greek, Mongol, and Islamic empires. It has experienced prolonged conflict, including Soviet invasion, civil war, Taliban rule, and recent international military involvement.
current_conflicts: Ongoing internal conflicts involving Taliban governance, resistance groups, and regional instability continue to affect security and humanitarian conditions.

commentary.inflation_management: Afghanistan's inflation is volatile and externally driven rather than managed by a conventional monetary framework. The food-and-fuel shock of 2008 pushed inflation to 26.4%, followed by sharp deflation of -6.8% in 2009 as commodity prices collapsed. After the 2021 Taliban takeover and the freezing of central bank reserves and aid, the economy contracted sharply (GDP fell from $20.1bn in 2020 to $14.3bn in 2021) and inflation ran at 10.6% in 2022 before swinging to deflation of -7.7% in 2023 and -4.3% in 2024 as demand collapsed and the afghani held firm under tight controls. The IMF projects 2.9% inflation for 2025, but with the central bank cut off from the international system there is no credible inflation-targeting regime in place.
commentary.debt_management: Public debt has stayed exceptionally low throughout the period, falling from 23.0% of GDP in 2006 to just 8.0% in the 2025 projection, because the state was financed by foreign grants rather than borrowing and ran up arrears rather than market debt. The 2021 collapse briefly lifted the ratio to 11.1% on the smaller GDP base, but there was no borrowing binge afterward. This is not a story of fiscal virtue so much as of a state that could not access capital markets and is now under sanctions; debt sustainability is moot while the government remains unrecognized and aid-dependent.

key_events.event: Global food-and-fuel price spike drove inflation to 26.4%.
NATO combat mission ended and a disputed presidential election created a unity government, slowing aid-backed growth.
COVID-19 disrupted trade and aid flows; GDP stalled at $20.1bn.
US withdrawal and Taliban takeover in August; GDP collapsed by roughly 30%, reserves were frozen and aid suspended.
Humanitarian crisis and demand collapse produced deflation (-7.7% in 2023) even as poverty deepened.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The outlook hinges on politics, not economics: recognition, sanctions relief, and resumed aid would stabilize output, while continued isolation keeps the economy in a low-level equilibrium with periodic deflation and humanitarian need. GDP is projected to recover only to $19.7bn by 2025, still below 2019 levels. Any upside depends on trade corridors and agriculture; the downside risk is renewed conflict or further isolation. Uncertainty is very high and data quality is poor.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
